Meshach
mē´shak
n. (the Babylonian name given to Mishael, one of Daniel's three companions)
A Babylonian name imposed on a Hebrew captive. His given name Mishael meant ‘who is what God is?’ — and the new name, bound to a heathen deity, could not unmake the confession the old one carried.

Biblical Definition

Meshach is the name the prince of the eunuchs laid on Mishael, one of the four young men of Judah carried to Babylon with Daniel. The renaming was policy: strip the Hebrew name that confessed the LORD, fit the young man with a name honouring Babylon's gods, feed him the king's meat, teach him the Chaldean tongue, and in three years the captive is a courtier. It worked on everything except the man. When Nebuchadnezzar set up the golden image and the whole plain fell down at the sound of the music, Meshach stood with Shadrach and Abednego. Their answer to the king is one of the high points of Scripture: they were not careful to answer him in the matter, their God was able to deliver them, and He would deliver them — but if not, they would still not serve his gods nor worship the golden image. They were cast bound into a furnace heated sevenfold, and the king rose up astonished to see a fourth in the fire. Nebuchadnezzar himself pronounced the verdict: they had yielded their bodies rather than serve any god except their own God.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) does not enter Meshach; the name is fixed by the book of Daniel as the Babylonian style of Mishael.

expand to see more

The proper name is not entered in Webster's 1828 dictionary.

MESHACH. The Chaldee name given to Mishael, of the children of Judah, in the court of Nebuchadnezzar.

Daniel 1:7 records the renaming of all four young men on their entrance into the king's service.

Mishael signifies, Who is what God is?

With Shadrach and Abednego he was cast into the burning fiery furnace and delivered unhurt.

Key Scripture

Dan 1:7 — "Unto whom the prince of the eunuchs gave names: for he gave unto Daniel the name of Belteshazzar; and to Hananiah, of Shadrach; and to Mishael, of Meshach; and to Azariah, of Abednego."

Dan 3:16 — "Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, answered and said to the king, O Nebuchadnezzar, we are not careful to answer thee in this matter."

Dan 3:17 — "If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king."

Dan 3:28 — "Then Nebuchadnezzar spake, and said, Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who hath sent his angel, and delivered his servants that trusted in him, and have changed the king's word, and yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God."

Modern Corruption

The furnace is retold as a promise that faith always spares the faithful, which is exactly the half these three refused to claim.

expand to see more

The story is commonly preached as a guarantee: trust God and the fire will not touch you. That reading has to cut the sentence in half. Meshach and his companions said their God was able to deliver, and that He would — and then added the words that make the confession worth anything at all: but if not, we will still not serve thy gods. They committed themselves before they knew the outcome, and they bound themselves to obedience in either case. Strip the second half away and the courage becomes a wager on a rescue, which is not faith but calculation.

The recovery is to preach both halves. God is able; that is not in doubt and never was. Whether He delivers in this instance is His to determine, and the believer's duty does not move with the answer. Hebrews sets the two side by side without embarrassment — some quenched the violence of fire, and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance. Meshach walked out of the furnace with not a hair singed; other saints have walked into fires they did not walk out of, and the same faith carried them. Nebuchadnezzar named the thing precisely: they yielded their bodies.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic Meyshak (H4335), Meshach; Hebrew Mishael (H4332), ‘who is what God is?’; Aramaic attun nura, the burning fiery furnace.

expand to see more

Aramaic Meyshak (H4335) — Meshach, the Babylonian name; Daniel 1:7, Daniel 3:16.

Hebrew Mishael (H4332) — Mishael, who is what God is?; Daniel 1:6-7.

Aramaic attun (H861) — a furnace; Daniel 3:6, Daniel 3:17.

Aramaic tselem (H6755) — the golden image set up in the plain of Dura; Daniel 3:1.

Hananiah became Shadrach and Azariah became Abednego in the same renaming.

Usage

"“We are not careful to answer thee in this matter” — no deliberation was required."

"“But if not” — the clause that makes the confession faith and not a wager."

"“Yielded their bodies” — Nebuchadnezzar's own account of what he had seen."
